notes.h: Functions, graphs and the standard economic forms
notes.body:
A function f: X → Y assigns exactly one output to each input. Economists use functions to describe relationships such as demand Q = D(P), cost C(q) and utility U(x, y). Key terms:
- Domain and range: the permitted inputs and the resulting outputs. Economic variables are often restricted to be non-negative.
- Inverse function: if f is strictly monotonic, f⁻¹ exists. Economists usually plot the inverse demand curve P = D⁻¹(Q), with price on the vertical axis.
- Composite function: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)), for example revenue as a function of labour through output.

Standard forms:
- Linear: y = a + bx, with slope b and intercept a. Two linear equations can be solved simultaneously, as in finding a market equilibrium.
- Quadratic: y = ax² + bx + c, with roots x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a and turning point at x = −b/2a. Total revenue under linear demand is quadratic.
- Power and Cobb-Douglas: y = Ax^a. A rectangular hyperbola y = k/x describes unit-elastic demand.
- Exponential and logarithmic: y = e^x and y = ln x are inverses. Continuous growth is y(t) = y₀e^(rt). Useful rules: ln(ab) = ln a + ln b, ln(a^n) = n ln a.

Functions of two variables can be drawn as level curves, the sets where f(x, y) = k. Indifference curves and isoquants are level curves.

Properties used throughout economics:
- Monotonicity: increasing or decreasing.
- Concavity and convexity: f is concave if the chord between any two points lies on or below the graph. Concave production functions reflect diminishing returns.
- Homogeneity: f(tx, ty) = t^k f(x, y), homogeneous of degree k. Cobb-Douglas Ax^a y^b is homogeneous of degree a + b.

Worked example: demand Q = 100 − 2P and supply Q = 3P − 20. Setting them equal gives 5P = 120, so P = 24 and Q = 52. Inverse demand is P = 50 − Q/2, so total revenue is TR = 50Q − Q²/2. This quadratic has its maximum at Q = 50, where P = 25.

Common pitfalls:
- Confusing a demand function with its inverse when reading slopes off a graph.
- Assuming every function has an inverse; it must be one-to-one.
- Treating ln(a + b) as ln a + ln b.
- Calling a function convex when it is quasi-convex; these are different properties, and quasi-concavity is what indifference curves need.

notes.h: Differentiation: rules, partial derivatives and elasticities
notes.body:
The derivative f'(x) = lim (h → 0) [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h measures the instantaneous rate of change, the slope of the tangent. In economics, "marginal" means derivative: marginal cost is C'(q) and marginal revenue is R'(q).

Rules:
- Power rule: d/dx(x^n) = nx^(n−1).
- Sum and constant multiple rules.
- Product rule: (uv)' = u'v + uv'.
- Quotient rule: (u/v)' = (u'v − uv')/v².
- Chain rule: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))·g'(x).
- Exponential and log: d/dx(e^x) = e^x; d/dx(ln x) = 1/x; d/dx(a^x) = a^x ln a.

Elasticity is the ratio of percentage changes: ε = (dy/dx)(x/y) = d ln y/d ln x. For y = Ax^b the elasticity is constant and equal to b. With revenue R = P·Q(P), dR/dP = Q(1 + ε), so revenue rises with price when demand is inelastic (|ε| < 1).

Partial derivatives: for f(x, y), ∂f/∂x is the derivative with y held fixed. Examples are marginal products and marginal utilities. Second-order partials fₓₓ, fᵧᵧ and fₓᵧ are collected in the Hessian matrix. Young's theorem says fₓᵧ = fᵧₓ for functions with continuous second partials.

Total differential: df = fₓ dx + fᵧ dy. Setting df = 0 along a level curve gives the implicit function rule dy/dx = −fₓ/fᵧ. This is how the MRS and MRTS are derived.

Euler's theorem: if f is homogeneous of degree k, then x·fₓ + y·fᵧ = k·f. With constant returns (k = 1), paying each input its marginal product exactly exhausts output.

Worked example: q = 10K^0.4 L^0.6. MPL = 6K^0.4 L^(−0.4) and MPK = 4K^(−0.6) L^0.6. MRTS = MPL/MPK = 1.5K/L. Euler: K·MPK + L·MPL = 4q/10 + 6q/10 = q.

Approximation: Δy ≈ f'(x)Δx for small changes. A second-order Taylor expansion adds ½f''(x)Δx².

Common pitfalls:
- Forgetting the chain rule's inner derivative, e.g. d/dx e^(3x) = 3e^(3x).
- Treating elasticity as a slope; it is unit-free and usually varies along a linear demand curve.
- Mixing up partial and total derivatives when variables depend on each other.
- Sign errors in the implicit function rule: remember the minus sign.

notes.h: Unconstrained optimisation in one and several variables
notes.body:
Optimisation is at the heart of economics: firms maximise profit and consumers maximise utility. Without constraints, the method is to find stationary points and then classify them.

One variable:
- First-order condition (FOC): f'(x*) = 0.
- Second-order condition (SOC): f''(x*) < 0 gives a local maximum and f''(x*) > 0 a local minimum. If f''(x*) = 0 the test is inconclusive, so check higher derivatives or the sign of f' either side. A point of inflection is possible.
- Global results: if f is concave everywhere, any stationary point is a global maximum. Also check endpoints when the domain is bounded, and corner solutions such as zero output.

Two variables, f(x, y):
- FOCs: fₓ = 0 and fᵧ = 0.
- Hessian H = [[fₓₓ, fₓᵧ], [fₓᵧ, fᵧᵧ]].
- Local maximum if fₓₓ < 0 and |H| = fₓₓfᵧᵧ − fₓᵧ² > 0. Local minimum if fₓₓ > 0 and |H| > 0. Saddle point if |H| < 0. Inconclusive if |H| = 0.
- With n variables, use the leading principal minors. They alternate in sign starting negative for a maximum (negative definite) and are all positive for a minimum (positive definite).

Economic applications: a profit-maximising firm sets MR = MC with MC cutting MR from below. A multi-product or multi-plant firm sets marginal revenue equal to each plant's marginal cost. A firm choosing inputs sets the value of the marginal product equal to the input price: p·MPL = w.

Worked example: a firm sells two goods with profit π = 40x + 60y − x² − xy − 2y². FOCs: πₓ = 40 − 2x − y = 0 and πᵧ = 60 − x − 4y = 0. Solving gives x = 100/7 ≈ 14.29 and y = 80/7 ≈ 11.43. Hessian: πₓₓ = −2, πᵧᵧ = −4, πₓᵧ = −1, so |H| = 8 − 1 = 7 > 0 with πₓₓ < 0. This is a maximum, and since the Hessian is constant and negative definite it is global. Substituting back, maximum profit = 4,400/7 ≈ 628.6.

The envelope theorem: when a parameter changes, the change in the maximised value equals the partial derivative of the objective with respect to that parameter, evaluated at the optimum. The indirect effect through the choice variables vanishes because of the FOCs.

Common pitfalls:
- Stopping at the FOC without checking the SOC.
- Using fₓₓ < 0 alone in two variables; |H| > 0 is also needed.
- Ignoring corner solutions and non-negativity.
- Calling a local maximum global without a concavity argument.

notes.h: Constrained optimisation: Lagrange multipliers and Kuhn–Tucker
notes.body:
Economic agents optimise subject to constraints, such as budgets, technology or resources. With an equality constraint g(x, y) = c, the Lagrange method is:

ℒ = f(x, y) + λ[c − g(x, y)]

First-order conditions: ℒₓ = fₓ − λgₓ = 0, ℒᵧ = fᵧ − λgᵧ = 0, and ℒ_λ = c − g(x, y) = 0. Dividing the first two gives fₓ/fᵧ = gₓ/gᵧ, the tangency between a level curve of f and the constraint. In consumer theory this is MRS = pₓ/pᵧ.

Interpreting λ: by the envelope theorem, λ* = dV*/dc, the rate at which the optimal value rises as the constraint is relaxed. In utility maximisation λ is the marginal utility of income. In cost minimisation it is marginal cost. In production planning it is the shadow price of a resource.

Second-order conditions use the bordered Hessian. With two variables and one constraint:
|H̄| = det [[0, gₓ, gᵧ], [gₓ, ℒₓₓ, ℒₓᵧ], [gᵧ, ℒₓᵧ, ℒᵧᵧ]].
|H̄| > 0 indicates a local maximum and |H̄| < 0 a local minimum. If the objective is quasi-concave and the constraint is linear, the tangency point is a maximum.

Worked example: maximise U = x^0.5 y^0.5 subject to 2x + 8y = 80. Tangency gives MRS = y/x = 2/8, so x = 4y. Substituting, 8y + 8y = 80, so y = 5 and x = 20. Then U = √100 = 10. From ℒₓ = 0.5x^(−0.5) y^0.5 − 2λ = 0, λ = 0.5 × √(5/20)/2 = 0.125. Check: indirect utility is v = m/(2√(pₓpᵧ)) = m/8, so dv/dm = 1/8.

Inequality constraints (Kuhn–Tucker): maximise f subject to g(x) ≤ c and x ≥ 0. The conditions are:
- ∂ℒ/∂xᵢ ≤ 0, xᵢ ≥ 0, with complementary slackness xᵢ·∂ℒ/∂xᵢ = 0.
- λ ≥ 0, g(x) ≤ c, and λ(c − g(x)) = 0.
A slack constraint has λ = 0; a positive shadow price means the constraint binds. These conditions handle corner solutions such as perfect substitutes, quasi-linear preferences with low income, or rationing.

Common pitfalls:
- Dropping the constraint equation from the FOCs.
- Misreading λ's sign. With the form f + λ(c − g), λ ≥ 0 for a maximum with a binding ≤ constraint.
- Applying tangency where the optimum is at a corner.
- Getting the bordered Hessian sign rule backwards: for a two-variable maximum it is positive.

notes.h: Integration: antiderivatives, areas and economic applications
notes.body:
Integration reverses differentiation. If F'(x) = f(x), then ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C, where C is an arbitrary constant. The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a) gives the signed area under f between a and b (the fundamental theorem of calculus).

Standard results:
- ∫x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n + 1) + C, for n ≠ −1.
- ∫(1/x)dx = ln|x| + C.
- ∫e^(kx)dx = e^(kx)/k + C.
- Integration is linear: ∫(af + bg) = a∫f + b∫g.

Techniques:
- Substitution (reversing the chain rule): ∫f(g(x))g'(x)dx = ∫f(u)du with u = g(x).
- Integration by parts (reversing the product rule): ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Choose u to become simpler when differentiated.

Economic applications:
- Recovering totals from marginals: total cost C(q) = ∫MC dq + FC, where the constant of integration is fixed cost. Total revenue from MR has zero constant, since R(0) = 0.
- Consumer surplus: CS = ∫₀^Q* D⁻¹(q)dq − P*Q*, or equivalently ∫ from P* to the choke price of D(p)dp.
- Producer surplus: PS = P*Q* − ∫₀^Q* S⁻¹(q)dq.
- Present value of a continuous income stream: PV = ∫₀^T R(t)e^(−rt)dt. For constant R this equals (R/r)(1 − e^(−rT)), which tends to R/r as T → ∞.
- Capital accumulation: K(T) − K(0) = ∫₀^T I(t)dt.
- Lorenz curves and the Gini coefficient: G = 1 − 2∫₀¹ L(x)dx.

Worked example: inverse demand P = 60 − 2Q with market price 20. Then Q* = 20 and CS = ∫₀²⁰(60 − 2q)dq − 400 = [60q − q²] from 0 to 20 − 400 = 800 − 400 = 400. This matches the triangle ½ × 20 × 40.

Improper integrals have an infinite limit and converge only if the limit exists. For example, ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) dx converges if and only if p > 1.

Common pitfalls:
- Forgetting the constant of integration, or giving it the wrong economic meaning.
- Using ∫x⁻¹dx = x⁰/0; the correct antiderivative is ln|x|.
- Sign errors when the function goes below the axis; signed area is not total area.
- Mixing up price and quantity integrals when computing surplus.

Matrices let us write systems of linear equations compactly as Ax = b, where A is the coefficient matrix, x the vector of unknowns and b the constants. They are used in multi-market equilibrium, input-output models, econometrics and second-order conditions.

Operations:
- Addition needs matrices of the same dimensions. Multiplication AB needs the number of columns of A to equal the number of rows of B. Multiplication is generally not commutative: AB ≠ BA.
- The transpose Aᵀ swaps rows and columns, and (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ.
- The identity matrix I satisfies AI = IA = A.

Determinants: for a 2×2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], det = ad − bc. For 3×3 matrices, use cofactor (Laplace) expansion along any row or column. A is invertible (non-singular) if and only if det A ≠ 0. Equivalently, its rows are linearly independent and it has full rank.

Inverse: A⁻¹ = adj(A)/det A, where adj is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. For 2×2, A⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc))[[d, −b], [−c, a]]. Then x = A⁻¹b.

Cramer's rule: xᵢ = det Aᵢ/det A, where Aᵢ replaces column i of A with b. It is useful in comparative statics when only one variable is needed.

Solutions of Ax = b:
- det A ≠ 0: a unique solution.
- det A = 0: either no solution (inconsistent) or infinitely many, depending on the rank of the augmented matrix (the Rouché–Capelli theorem).

Leontief input-output model: x = Ax + d, where A holds the technical coefficients and d is final demand. The solution is x = (I − A)⁻¹d. (I − A)⁻¹ is the Leontief inverse, and its entries show the total (direct and indirect) output needed per unit of final demand.

Definiteness: a symmetric matrix is negative definite if its leading principal minors alternate in sign, starting negative. This is the second-order condition for a maximum.

Worked example: two markets with excess demands 10 − 2P₁ + P₂ = 0 and 5 + P₁ − 3P₂ = 0. In matrix form, [[2, −1], [−1, 3]]P = [10, 5]ᵀ. det = 6 − 1 = 5. By Cramer: P₁ = (10×3 − (−1)×5)/5 = 35/5 = 7 and P₂ = (2×5 − (−1)×10)/5 = 20/5 = 4. Check: 10 − 14 + 4 = 0 and 5 + 7 − 12 = 0.

Common pitfalls:
- Assuming AB = BA.
- Inverting a singular matrix.
- Sign errors in cofactors (the checkerboard pattern of + and −).
- In Cramer's rule, replacing a row instead of a column.

notes.h: Difference and differential equations: dynamics and stability
notes.body:
Dynamic models describe how variables evolve over time. Discrete time uses difference equations; continuous time uses differential equations.

First-order linear difference equation: yₜ₊₁ = ayₜ + b.
- Steady state (fixed point): y* = b/(1 − a), for a ≠ 1.
- Solution: yₜ = y* + (y₀ − y*)aᵗ.
- Stability: converges to y* if |a| < 1. It oscillates if a < 0 and moves monotonically if a > 0. It diverges if |a| > 1.

Cobweb model: demand Qₜ = α − βPₜ and supply Qₜ = γ + δPₜ₋₁, because producers base output on last period's price. Market clearing gives Pₜ = (α − γ)/β − (δ/β)Pₜ₋₁. Since a = −δ/β < 0, prices oscillate. They converge if δ < β, i.e. if quantity supplied responds less to price than quantity demanded does. In the usual diagram with price on the vertical axis, this means the supply curve is steeper than the demand curve.

First-order linear differential equation: dy/dt + ay = b.
- Steady state: y* = b/a.
- Solution: y(t) = y* + (y(0) − y*)e^(−at).
- Stable if a > 0.
More generally, dy/dt + a(t)y = b(t) is solved with the integrating factor e^(∫a dt). Separable equations dy/dt = g(y)h(t) are solved by ∫dy/g(y) = ∫h(t)dt.

Phase diagrams: for an autonomous equation dy/dt = f(y), steady states satisfy f(y*) = 0. The steady state is stable if f'(y*) < 0. The Solow model, k' = s·f(k) − (n + δ)k, has a stable positive steady state because s·f(k) is concave.

Second-order equations: y'' + a₁y' + a₂y = b. The characteristic equation r² + a₁r + a₂ = 0 has roots r₁ and r₂.
- Real distinct roots: y = y* + A₁e^(r₁t) + A₂e^(r₂t).
- Repeated root: y = y* + (A₁ + A₂t)e^(rt).
- Complex roots h ± vi: y = y* + e^(ht)(A₁cos vt + A₂sin vt).
- Stable if and only if every root has a negative real part.
For difference equations the corresponding condition is that every root has modulus less than 1. Samuelson's (1939) multiplier-accelerator model uses a second-order difference equation to produce cycles.

Worked example: dP/dt = k(D − S) with D = 40 − 2P, S = 10 + 4P and k = 0.5. Then dP/dt = 0.5(30 − 6P) = 15 − 3P. P* = 5 and P(t) = 5 + (P(0) − 5)e^(−3t), which is stable.

Common pitfalls:
- Mixing up the stability conditions: |a| < 1 in discrete time versus a negative root (or a > 0 in dy/dt + ay = b) in continuous time.
- Forgetting the oscillation that comes from a negative coefficient in difference equations.
- Leaving out the steady-state (particular) solution.
- Using initial conditions before writing down the general solution.

cards.f: What condition must a function satisfy to have an inverse?
cards.b: It must be one-to-one (injective) on its domain. A strictly monotonic function always has an inverse.

cards.f: Where is the turning point of y = ax² + bx + c?
cards.b: At x = −b/(2a). It is a maximum if a < 0 and a minimum if a > 0.

cards.f: State the quadratic formula.
cards.b: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a). The discriminant b² − 4ac shows whether there are two, one or no real roots.

cards.f: Define a function homogeneous of degree k.
cards.b: f(tx, ty) = t^k f(x, y) for all t > 0. For example, Ax^a y^b is homogeneous of degree a + b.

cards.f: Simplify ln(x³y/z).
cards.b: 3 ln x + ln y − ln z.

cards.f: Define a concave function.
cards.b: f is concave if f(λx + (1 − λ)y) ≥ λf(x) + (1 − λ)f(y) for all x, y and λ in [0, 1]: the chord lies on or below the graph.

cards.f: Concave versus quasi-concave?
cards.b: Quasi-concavity only requires upper level sets {x: f(x) ≥ k} to be convex. Every concave function is quasi-concave, but not vice versa: f = xy on the positive quadrant is quasi-concave but not concave.

cards.f: What is a level curve?
cards.b: The set of points where a function of two variables takes a constant value, f(x, y) = k. Indifference curves and isoquants are level curves.

cards.f: Continuous growth formula and doubling time?
cards.b: y(t) = y₀e^(rt). The doubling time is ln 2/r ≈ 0.693/r, the basis of the rule of 70.

cards.f: Why does a rectangular hyperbola P = k/Q represent unit-elastic demand?
cards.b: Total spending P·Q = k is constant at every price, so a 1% price rise leads to a 1% fall in quantity.

cards.f: State the chain rule.
cards.b: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))·g'(x): differentiate the outer function and multiply by the derivative of the inner function.

cards.f: State the quotient rule.
cards.b: (u/v)' = (u'v − uv')/v².

cards.f: Differentiate y = e^(2x) ln x.
cards.b: Product rule: y' = 2e^(2x) ln x + e^(2x)/x.

cards.f: Point elasticity of y with respect to x?
cards.b: ε = (dy/dx)(x/y) = d ln y/d ln x: the percentage change in y per 1% change in x.

cards.f: Elasticity of y = Ax^b?
cards.b: Constant and equal to b at every point.

cards.f: Implicit function rule for a level curve f(x, y) = k?
cards.b: dy/dx = −fₓ/fᵧ, from setting the total differential fₓdx + fᵧdy to zero.

cards.f: State Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions.
cards.b: If f is homogeneous of degree k, then Σ xᵢ ∂f/∂xᵢ = k·f(x). With constant returns, paying each input its marginal product exhausts output.

cards.f: State Young's theorem.
cards.b: If the second-order partial derivatives are continuous, the cross-partials are equal: fₓᵧ = fᵧₓ.

cards.f: How does total revenue respond to price, in terms of elasticity?
cards.b: dR/dP = Q(1 + ε), where ε < 0. Revenue rises with price if demand is inelastic (|ε| < 1) and falls if it is elastic.

cards.f: Partial derivatives of f = x²y³ + 4xy?
cards.b: fₓ = 2xy³ + 4y and fᵧ = 3x²y² + 4x.

cards.f: First- and second-order conditions for a maximum of f(x)?
cards.b: FOC: f'(x*) = 0. SOC: f''(x*) < 0. If f''(x*) = 0 the test is inconclusive.

cards.f: Second-order conditions for a maximum of f(x, y)?
cards.b: fₓₓ < 0 and |H| = fₓₓfᵧᵧ − fₓᵧ² > 0, i.e. the Hessian is negative definite.

cards.f: What does |H| < 0 at a stationary point of f(x, y) indicate?
cards.b: A saddle point: neither a maximum nor a minimum.

cards.f: When is a stationary point a global maximum?
cards.b: When the function is concave over a convex domain. Then any stationary point is a global maximum.

cards.f: State the envelope theorem (unconstrained case).
cards.b: dV*/dα = ∂f(x*, α)/∂α: the effect of a parameter on the maximised value equals its direct effect, because the indirect effects vanish by the FOCs.

cards.f: Profit-maximisation conditions for a firm with two plants?
cards.b: MR(Q) = MC₁(q₁) = MC₂(q₂): output is shared so that marginal costs are equal across plants, and both equal marginal revenue.

cards.f: Find and classify the stationary points of f(x) = x³ − 3x.
cards.b: f'(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = ±1. f''(x) = 6x, so x = 1 is a local minimum (f = −2) and x = −1 a local maximum (f = 2).

cards.f: Leading principal minor test for a maximum with n variables?
cards.b: The leading principal minors of the Hessian alternate in sign, starting negative: |H₁| < 0, |H₂| > 0, |H₃| < 0, and so on.

cards.f: Optimal labour choice for a price-taking firm?
cards.b: Set the value of the marginal product equal to the wage: p·MPL = w.

cards.f: Why should you check corner solutions?
cards.b: When variables must be non-negative or lie in a bounded set, the optimum may be on the boundary, where the derivative need not be zero.

cards.f: Set up the Lagrangian for max f(x, y) subject to g(x, y) = c.
cards.b: ℒ = f(x, y) + λ[c − g(x, y)]. Set ℒₓ = ℒᵧ = ℒ_λ = 0.

cards.f: Interpret the Lagrange multiplier.
cards.b: λ* = dV*/dc: the change in the optimal value per unit relaxation of the constraint, i.e. the shadow price of the constraint.

cards.f: What is λ in utility maximisation and in cost minimisation?
cards.b: In utility maximisation, the marginal utility of income. In cost minimisation, marginal cost.

cards.f: What tangency condition comes from the Lagrange FOCs?
cards.b: fₓ/fᵧ = gₓ/gᵧ: the level curve of the objective is tangent to the constraint.

cards.f: Bordered Hessian sign rule with two variables and one constraint?
cards.b: |H̄| > 0 gives a local maximum and |H̄| < 0 a local minimum.

cards.f: State complementary slackness.
cards.b: λ(c − g(x)) = 0: either the constraint binds or its multiplier is zero. Likewise xᵢ·∂ℒ/∂xᵢ = 0 for non-negativity constraints.

cards.f: When are Kuhn–Tucker conditions needed rather than Lagrange?
cards.b: When constraints are inequalities or variables must be non-negative, so the optimum may be at a corner or a constraint may be slack.

cards.f: Maximise U = xy subject to x + 2y = 40.
cards.b: Tangency y/x = 1/2 gives x = 2y, so 4y = 40: y = 10, x = 20, U = 200.

cards.f: Why is the solution to max x^a y^b subject to a linear budget a maximum?
cards.b: Cobb-Douglas utility is quasi-concave and the budget set is convex, so the tangency point is the maximum.

cards.f: ∫x^n dx?

cards.b: ln|x| + C.

cards.f: ∫e^(kx) dx?
cards.b: e^(kx)/k + C, for k ≠ 0.

cards.f: State the integration by parts formula.
cards.b: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Choose u to become simpler when differentiated.

cards.f: How do you recover total cost from marginal cost?
cards.b: C(q) = ∫MC(q)dq + C, where the constant of integration is fixed cost.

cards.f: Consumer surplus as an integral?
cards.b: CS = ∫₀^Q* P(q)dq − P*Q*, where P(q) is inverse demand.

cards.f: Present value of a constant stream R for T years at continuous rate r?
cards.b: PV = ∫₀^T Re^(−rt)dt = (R/r)(1 − e^(−rT)), tending to R/r as T → ∞.

cards.f: When does ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) dx converge?
cards.b: If and only if p > 1, when it equals 1/(p − 1).

cards.f: Gini coefficient in terms of the Lorenz curve L(x)?
cards.b: G = 1 − 2∫₀¹ L(x)dx: twice the area between the equality line and the Lorenz curve.

cards.f: Evaluate ∫₀² 3x² dx.
cards.b: [x³] from 0 to 2 = 8.

cards.f: Determinant of [[a, b], [c, d]]?
cards.b: ad − bc.

cards.f: Inverse of a 2×2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]]?
cards.b: (1/(ad − bc))[[d, −b], [−c, a]], provided ad − bc ≠ 0.

cards.f: When is a square matrix invertible?
cards.b: If and only if its determinant is non-zero. Equivalently, it has full rank and linearly independent rows and columns.

cards.f: State Cramer's rule.
cards.b: For Ax = b with det A ≠ 0, xᵢ = det Aᵢ/det A, where Aᵢ is A with column i replaced by b.

cards.f: Is matrix multiplication commutative?
cards.b: No. In general AB ≠ BA, and one product may exist while the other does not.

cards.f: Transpose of a product?
cards.b: (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ.

cards.f: Solution of the Leontief input-output model?
cards.b: x = (I − A)⁻¹d, where A holds technical coefficients and d is final demand. The Leontief inverse gives total direct and indirect requirements.

cards.f: Possible outcomes for Ax = b when det A = 0?
cards.b: No solution or infinitely many, depending on whether rank of A equals rank of the augmented matrix [A | b].

cards.f: When is a symmetric matrix positive definite?
cards.b: When all its leading principal minors are positive, equivalently all its eigenvalues are positive.

cards.f: Effect of swapping two rows on a determinant?
cards.b: It changes the sign of the determinant. Multiplying one row by k multiplies the determinant by k.

cards.f: Steady state and solution of yₜ₊₁ = ayₜ + b?
cards.b: y* = b/(1 − a) for a ≠ 1, and yₜ = y* + (y₀ − y*)aᵗ.

cards.f: Stability condition for yₜ₊₁ = ayₜ + b?
cards.b: Stable if |a| < 1. Oscillating if a < 0, monotonic if a > 0.

cards.f: Solution of dy/dt + ay = b?
cards.b: y(t) = b/a + (y(0) − b/a)e^(−at), stable if a > 0.

cards.f: Stability condition in the cobweb model?
cards.b: With demand slope −β and supply slope δ (lagged price), prices oscillate and converge if δ/β < 1, i.e. supply responds less to price than demand does. With price on the vertical axis, the supply curve is steeper than the demand curve.

cards.f: Stability of a steady state of dy/dt = f(y)?
cards.b: Stable if f'(y*) < 0, unstable if f'(y*) > 0.

cards.f: Solution of y'' + a₁y' + a₂y = 0 with complex roots h ± vi?
cards.b: y = e^(ht)(A₁ cos vt + A₂ sin vt): cycles that dampen if h < 0 and explode if h > 0.

cards.f: Stability condition for a second-order differential equation?
cards.b: Both characteristic roots must have negative real parts. For y'' + a₁y' + a₂y = b this means a₁ > 0 and a₂ > 0.

cards.f: Stability condition for a second-order difference equation?
cards.b: Both roots of the characteristic equation must have modulus less than 1.

cards.f: What is a separable differential equation and how is it solved?
cards.b: One of the form dy/dt = g(y)h(t). Solve by integrating ∫dy/g(y) = ∫h(t)dt.

cards.f: Why is the Solow steady state stable?
cards.b: In k' = s·f(k) − (n + δ)k, concavity of f makes s·f(k) cross the line (n + δ)k from above, so k' > 0 below k* and k' < 0 above it.

cards.f: What is the shadow price of a constraint that does not bind?
cards.b: Zero. Relaxing a slack constraint does not change the optimal value, so complementary slackness sets its multiplier to 0.

cards.f: Why does the Lagrange tangency method fail for U = x + y?
cards.b: The indifference curves are straight lines, so they are generally not tangent to the budget line; the optimum is a corner where only the cheaper good is bought.

cards.f: ∫f'(x)/f(x) dx?
cards.b: ln|f(x)| + C, by the substitution u = f(x).

cards.f: Determinant of a triangular matrix?
cards.b: The product of its diagonal entries.

questions.q: Which expression equals ln(a²/b) for a, b > 0?
questions.why: Using ln(x/y) = ln x − ln y and ln(xⁿ) = n ln x gives 2 ln a − ln b.

questions.q: The production function f(K, L) = K^0.4 L^0.8 is homogeneous of degree:
questions.why: f(tK, tL) = t^0.4 t^0.8 f(K, L) = t^1.2 f(K, L), so it is homogeneous of degree 1.2 (increasing returns to scale).

questions.q: What is the derivative of y = e^(3x²)?
questions.why: By the chain rule, the derivative of the exponent 3x² is 6x, which multiplies e^(3x²).

questions.q: For the demand function Q = 200P^(−1.5), the price elasticity of demand at P = 4 is:
options: It cannot be found without Q
questions.why: For Q = AP^b the elasticity is constant and equal to b, so it is −1.5 at every price.

questions.q: At a stationary point of f(x, y), fₓₓ = 2, fᵧᵧ = 3 and fₓᵧ = 4. The point is:
questions.why: |H| = fₓₓfᵧᵧ − fₓᵧ² = 6 − 16 = −10 < 0, which indicates a saddle point even though fₓₓ > 0.

questions.q: A firm minimises cost subject to producing q units. At the optimum the Lagrange multiplier on the output constraint equals 12. This means:
options: Producing one more unit would raise minimum cost by about 12
The firm should cut output by 12 units
The marginal product of labour is 12
questions.why: By the envelope theorem λ = dC*/dq, so the multiplier on the output constraint is marginal cost.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₁³ 2x dx.
questions.why: The antiderivative is x², so the integral is 3² − 1² = 9 − 1 = 8.

questions.q: An asset pays a continuous income of £500 per year forever. With a continuous discount rate of 5%, its present value is:
questions.why: PV = ∫₀^∞ 500e^(−0.05t)dt = 500/0.05 = £10,000. The integral converges because the discount factor decays exponentially.

questions.q: A is a 2×3 matrix and B is a 3×4 matrix. Which statement is correct?
options: AB is 2×4 and BA is not defined
Both AB and BA are defined
Neither AB nor BA is defined
questions.why: AB needs columns of A (3) to equal rows of B (3) and gives a 2×4 matrix. BA would need 4 = 2, so it is not defined.

questions.q: For which value of k is the system 2x + ky = 5, 4x + 6y = 3 without a unique solution?
questions.why: The determinant 2×6 − 4k = 12 − 4k is zero when k = 3, so the coefficient matrix is singular. (Here the system is then inconsistent.)

questions.q: The difference equation yₜ₊₁ = −0.8yₜ + 9 has which behaviour?
questions.why: y* = 9/(1 + 0.8) = 5. Since a = −0.8 has |a| < 1 and is negative, the path oscillates around 5 while converging.

questions.q: Consider dy/dt = 0.3y − 6. Which statement is correct?
options: The steady state y = 20 is stable
The steady state y = 20 is unstable
The steady state y = −20 is stable
questions.why: Setting dy/dt = 0 gives y* = 20. Since d(dy/dt)/dy = 0.3 > 0, deviations grow exponentially, so the steady state is unstable.

questions.q: £5,000 is invested at an annual interest rate of 4% for 3 years. Find its final value with quarterly compounding and with continuous compounding, and explain the difference.
markScheme: Explains that more frequent compounding earns interest on interest sooner; continuous compounding is the limit
questions.modelAnswer: With quarterly compounding the rate per quarter is 1% and there are 12 quarters, so A = 5,000 × 1.01^12 ≈ £5,634.13. With continuous compounding A = 5,000e^(rt) = 5,000e^0.12 ≈ £5,637.48. The continuous value is slightly higher because interest is added to the balance immediately and itself earns interest. As the number of compounding periods n rises, (1 + r/n)^(nt) increases towards the limit e^(rt).

questions.q: Demand for a product is Q = 120 − 3P². Find the price elasticity of demand at P = 4, and state whether a small price cut would raise or lower total revenue.
markScheme: Demand is elastic (|ε| > 1), so a price cut raises revenue
questions.modelAnswer: Differentiating, dQ/dP = −6P, which equals −24 at P = 4. Quantity there is 120 − 3(16) = 72. The point elasticity is ε = (dQ/dP)(P/Q) = −24 × 4/72 = −4/3. Since |ε| > 1, demand is elastic: a 1% price cut raises quantity by about 1.33%, so total revenue rises. Formally, dR/dP = Q(1 + ε) = 72(1 − 4/3) = −24 < 0, so lowering the price increases revenue.

questions.q: A firm's production function is Q = K^0.5 L^0.25. Use implicit differentiation to find the slope of the isoquant at K = 20, L = 8, and state the firm's returns to scale.
markScheme: Exponents sum to 0.75 < 1, so decreasing returns to scale
questions.modelAnswer: Along an isoquant dQ = MPK·dK + MPL·dL = 0, so dK/dL = −MPL/MPK. Here MPL = 0.25K^0.5 L^(−0.75) and MPK = 0.5K^(−0.5) L^0.25. Their ratio is (0.25/0.5)(K/L) = 0.5K/L. At K = 20 and L = 8, dK/dL = −0.5 × 2.5 = −1.25. One more unit of labour lets the firm release 1.25 units of capital while keeping output constant. The exponents sum to 0.75 < 1, so the firm has decreasing returns to scale.

questions.q: A firm's profit function is π(q) = −q³/3 + 10q² − 64q − 50. Find and classify the stationary points and the profit-maximising output and profit.
questions.modelAnswer: Differentiating gives π'(q) = −q² + 20q − 64. Setting this to zero, q² − 20q + 64 = 0, which factorises as (q − 4)(q − 16) = 0. The second derivative is π''(q) = −2q + 20. At q = 4, π'' = 12 > 0, so this is a local minimum of profit, where MC cuts MR from above. At q = 16, π'' = −12 < 0, a local maximum. Profit there is −4,096/3 + 2,560 − 1,024 − 50 = 362/3 ≈ 120.67. This exceeds π(0) = −50, so q = 16 is the profit-maximising output.

questions.q: A firm produces q = K^0.5 L^0.5 and must produce q = 20. The wage is 8 and the rental rate is 2. Use the Lagrange method to find the cost-minimising inputs, the minimum cost and the value of the multiplier, and interpret it.
markScheme: ℒ = 8L + 2K + λ(20 − K^0.5 L^0.5) with correct FOCs
Ratio of FOCs gives K/L = 8/2, so K = 4L
questions.modelAnswer: Set ℒ = 8L + 2K + λ(20 − K^0.5 L^0.5). The FOCs are 8 = 0.5λK^0.5 L^(−0.5) and 2 = 0.5λK^(−0.5) L^0.5. Dividing them gives K/L = 4, so K = 4L. The constraint then gives √(4L²) = 2L = 20, so L = 10 and K = 40. Minimum cost is 8(10) + 2(40) = 160. From the first FOC, 8 = 0.5λ√4 = λ, so λ = 8. The multiplier is marginal cost: the cost function is C = 2q√(wr) = 8q, so producing one more unit raises minimum cost by 8.

questions.q: A firm's marginal cost is MC = 6q + 4 and its fixed cost is 30. Find the total cost function, the total cost of producing 10 units, and the extra cost of raising output from 10 to 12 units.
markScheme: Constant of integration equals fixed cost: TC = 3q² + 4q + 30
questions.modelAnswer: Integrating marginal cost gives TC = 3q² + 4q + C. The constant is the cost at zero output, which is fixed cost, so TC = 3q² + 4q + 30. At q = 10, TC = 300 + 40 + 30 = 370. The extra cost of moving from 10 to 12 units is the definite integral of MC between those outputs: [3q² + 4q] from 10 to 12 = (432 + 48) − (300 + 40) = 140. Fixed cost cancels, as it should, because it does not vary with output.

questions.q: Use integration by parts to evaluate ∫₀¹ x·eˣ dx.
markScheme: Chooses u = x, dv = eˣdx, so du = dx and v = eˣ
questions.modelAnswer: Let u = x and dv = eˣdx, so du = dx and v = eˣ. Integration by parts gives ∫x·eˣ dx = x·eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = x·eˣ − eˣ + C = (x − 1)eˣ + C. Evaluating between 0 and 1: at x = 1 the value is 0, and at x = 0 it is −1. The definite integral is therefore 0 − (−1) = 1. Choosing u = x works because it becomes simpler (a constant) when differentiated.

questions.q: Let A = [[2, 1], [5, 3]]. Find A⁻¹ and use it to solve 2x + y = 7, 5x + 3y = 18.
markScheme: y = −5(7) + 2(18) = 1, checked in the original equations
questions.modelAnswer: The determinant is 2 × 3 − 1 × 5 = 1, so A is invertible. Swapping the diagonal entries, changing the signs of the off-diagonal entries and dividing by 1 gives A⁻¹ = [[3, −1], [−5, 2]]. Then (x, y)ᵀ = A⁻¹(7, 18)ᵀ, so x = 21 − 18 = 3 and y = −35 + 36 = 1. Check: 2(3) + 1 = 7 and 5(3) + 3(1) = 18.

questions.q: Solve the difference equation yₜ = 0.6yₜ₋₁ + 8 with y₀ = 30. Find y₂ and describe the long-run behaviour.
markScheme: |0.6| < 1 and positive, so y converges monotonically to 20
questions.modelAnswer: The steady state solves y* = 0.6y* + 8, so y* = 8/0.4 = 20. The general solution is yₜ = y* + (y₀ − y*)(0.6)ᵗ = 20 + 10(0.6)ᵗ. Then y₂ = 20 + 10 × 0.36 = 23.6, which matches iterating directly: y₁ = 26 and y₂ = 23.6. Since the coefficient 0.6 lies between 0 and 1, the deviation from 20 shrinks by 40% each period without changing sign, so y falls monotonically towards 20.

questions.q: In a cobweb model, demand is Qₜ = 80 − 4Pₜ and supply is Qₜ = −10 + 2Pₜ₋₁. Derive the price path when P₀ = 19, find P₁ and P₂, and assess stability.
markScheme: |−0.5| < 1, so damped oscillations converge to 15; stable because supply responds less to price (dQ/dP = 2) than demand (|dQ/dP| = 4)
questions.modelAnswer: Setting demand equal to supply gives 80 − 4Pₜ = −10 + 2Pₜ₋₁, so Pₜ = 22.5 − 0.5Pₜ₋₁. The equilibrium satisfies P* = 22.5 − 0.5P*, so P* = 15 and Q* = 20. The solution is Pₜ = 15 + (19 − 15)(−0.5)ᵗ = 15 + 4(−0.5)ᵗ. So P₁ = 13 and P₂ = 16. The coefficient −0.5 is negative with modulus below 1: prices overshoot alternately above and below 15, but the deviations halve each period, so the market converges. This occurs because producers respond less strongly to price (slope 2) than consumers (slope 4).

questions.q:
Brightwater Juice faces weekly demand Q = 400 − 20P for its smoothies and has total cost TC = 960 + 4Q.

(a) Find the inverse demand function and total revenue as a function of Q. Find the output that maximises revenue and the price elasticity there. (4 marks)
(b) Write profit as a function of Q. Find the break-even outputs and the profit-maximising output, price and profit. (5 marks)
(c) Brightwater expects the demand intercept to grow by 5% per year, compounded annually. How many years until it doubles? How would the answer change with 5% continuous growth? (3 marks)
markScheme: TR = 20Q − Q²/20, maximised at Q = 200 (P = 10, TR = 2,000)
Break-even: Q² − 320Q + 19,200 = 0, giving Q = 80 or Q = 240
Annual compounding: 1.05ᵗ = 2, so t = ln 2/ln 1.05 ≈ 14.2 years
Continuous: t = ln 2/0.05 ≈ 13.9 years, shorter because growth compounds continuously
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Rearranging Q = 400 − 20P gives the inverse demand P = 20 − Q/20. Total revenue is TR = PQ = 20Q − Q²/20. This is a downward-opening quadratic with vertex at Q = −20/(2 × (−1/20)) = 200. There P = 10 and TR = 2,000. The elasticity is ε = (dQ/dP)(P/Q) = −20 × 10/200 = −1. Revenue is maximised exactly where demand is unit elastic, as MR = P(1 + 1/ε) = 0.

(b) Profit is π = TR − TC = 20Q − Q²/20 − 960 − 4Q = −Q²/20 + 16Q − 960. Setting π = 0 and multiplying by −20 gives Q² − 320Q + 19,200 = 0. The discriminant is 320² − 4 × 19,200 = 102,400 − 76,800 = 25,600 = 160², so Q = (320 ± 160)/2, giving Q = 80 or Q = 240. Between these outputs profit is positive. The maximum is at the vertex, Q = 16/(2 × 1/20) = 160, which lies midway between the roots. Price is 20 − 8 = £12 and profit is −1,280 + 2,560 − 960 = £320. Equivalently MR = 20 − Q/10 = 4 = MC gives Q = 160.

(c) With annual compounding the intercept is 400(1.05)ᵗ. Doubling requires 1.05ᵗ = 2, so t = ln 2/ln 1.05 = 0.6931/0.0488 ≈ 14.2 years. With continuous growth, 400e^(0.05t) doubles when 0.05t = ln 2, so t ≈ 13.9 years. Continuous compounding is slightly faster because growth builds on itself at every instant. The rule of 70 (70/5 = 14) is a good approximation to both.

questions.q:
A manufacturing firm has production function Q = 10K^0.4 L^0.6 and currently uses K = 32 and L = 32.

(a) Find output and the marginal products of capital and labour. (3 marks)
(b) Use the total differential to estimate the change in output if K rises by 2 and L falls by 1. (2 marks)
(c) Find the MRTS and interpret it. (2 marks)
(d) Verify Euler's theorem and explain its economic meaning. (2 marks)
(e) If K grows by 5% and L by 2% a year, estimate output growth and sign the second-order partial derivatives. (3 marks)
markScheme: Interpretation: one extra unit of labour replaces 1.5 units of capital
Q_LL = −0.24Q/L² < 0 and Q_KK = −0.24Q/K² < 0 (diminishing returns); Q_KL = 0.24Q/(KL) > 0 (complementary inputs)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) With K = L = 32, Q = 10 × 32^(0.4 + 0.6) = 320. For Cobb-Douglas, each marginal product equals the exponent times the average product: MPK = 0.4Q/K = 0.4 × 10 = 4 and MPL = 0.6Q/L = 6.

(b) The total differential is dQ = MPK·dK + MPL·dL = 4(2) + 6(−1) = 2. Output rises by about 2 units. The exact figure at (34, 31) is 10 × 34^0.4 × 31^0.6 ≈ 321.7, so the linear approximation is close.

(c) MRTS = MPL/MPK = (0.6/0.4)(K/L) = 1.5 at this point. The firm could use one more unit of labour and 1.5 fewer units of capital and keep output unchanged. The isoquant slope is dK/dL = −1.5.

(d) Q is homogeneous of degree 1, so Euler's theorem predicts K·MPK + L·MPL = Q. Indeed 32 × 4 + 32 × 6 = 128 + 192 = 320. If each input is paid its marginal product, as in competitive factor markets, total payments exactly exhaust output: capital receives 40% and labour 60%, and there is no pure profit.

(e) Taking logs and differentiating with respect to time gives Q̇/Q = 0.4(K̇/K) + 0.6(L̇/L), so output growth ≈ 0.4 × 5% + 0.6 × 2% = 3.2% a year, before any productivity growth. This is the basis of growth accounting. The second derivatives are Q_KK = 0.4(−0.6)Q/K² < 0 and Q_LL = 0.6(−0.4)Q/L² < 0, showing diminishing marginal returns to each input. The cross-partial Q_KL = 0.24Q/(KL) > 0, so more capital raises the marginal product of labour: the inputs are complements in production.

questions.q:
Halden Ltd produces two goods, x and y, with inverse demands Pₓ = 70 − 2x and Pᵧ = 90 − 3y. Production is linked, and the joint cost function is C = x² + xy + y² + 50.

(a) Write the profit function and find the profit-maximising outputs and prices. (5 marks)
(b) Show that this is a maximum and explain why it is global. (3 marks)
(c) Find maximum profit. (2 marks)
(d) The government imposes a per-unit tax t on good x. Using comparative statics, find dx*/dt, dy*/dt and dπ*/dt at t = 0, and explain the sign of dy*/dt. (5 marks)
markScheme: Solution x = 10, y = 10; prices Pₓ = 50, Pᵧ = 60
Hessian is constant and negative definite, so π is strictly concave and the maximum is global
Differentiating the FOCs with tax: 6dx + dy = −dt and dx + 8dy = 0
Explains dy*/dt > 0: the cost interaction means less x lowers the marginal cost of y (C_xy = 1 > 0)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Profit is revenue minus cost: π = (70 − 2x)x + (90 − 3y)y − x² − xy − y² − 50 = 70x + 90y − 3x² − 4y² − xy − 50. The FOCs are πₓ = 70 − 6x − y = 0 and πᵧ = 90 − x − 8y = 0. From the first, y = 70 − 6x. Substituting gives 90 − x − 560 + 48x = 0, so 47x = 470 and x = 10, y = 10. Prices are Pₓ = 70 − 20 = 50 and Pᵧ = 90 − 30 = 60.

(b) The Hessian is H = [[−6, −1], [−1, −8]]. Since πₓₓ = −6 < 0 and |H| = 48 − 1 = 47 > 0, H is negative definite and the stationary point is a maximum. Because π is quadratic, H is the same everywhere, so π is strictly concave and (10, 10) is the unique global maximum.

(c) π* = 700 + 900 − 300 − 400 − 100 − 50 = 750.

(d) A tax t per unit of x changes the first FOC to 70 − t − 6x − y = 0. Totally differentiating both FOCs gives −dt − 6dx − dy = 0 and −dx − 8dy = 0. So dx = −8dy, and substituting, 48dy − dy = dt, giving dy*/dt = 1/47 ≈ 0.021 and dx*/dt = −8/47 ≈ −0.170. (Cramer's rule on the Hessian gives the same answer.) By the envelope theorem, dπ*/dt = ∂π/∂t = −x* = −10: at the margin, profit falls by the tax paid on current output, because the induced output changes have no first-order effect.

Output of y rises because the goods are cost-linked: ∂²C/∂x∂y = 1 > 0, so producing less x lowers the marginal cost of y. The firm shifts production towards the untaxed good. The tax therefore spills over to the other market, which a single-market analysis would miss.

questions.q:
Sofia has utility U = ln x + 2 ln y, an income of £90, and faces prices pₓ = £2 and pᵧ = £3.

(a) Use the Lagrange method to find her optimal bundle and the value of λ. (5 marks)
(b) Show that λ equals the derivative of maximised utility with respect to income. (3 marks)
(c) Verify the second-order condition using the bordered Hessian. (3 marks)
(d) Good x is now rationed: Sofia may buy at most 10 units. Use the Kuhn–Tucker conditions to find her new bundle and the shadow price of the ration. (4 marks)
markScheme: ℒ = ln x + 2 ln y + λ(90 − 2x − 3y)
General demands x = m/(3pₓ), y = 2m/(3pᵧ); V(m) = ln(m/3pₓ) + 2 ln(2m/3pᵧ)
Bordered Hessian determinant = pₓ²(2/y²) + pᵧ²(1/x²) = 0.02 + 0.04 = 0.06 > 0, so a maximum
With the ration binding: x = 10, y = 70/3 ≈ 23.33
λ = 2/(3y) = 1/35; ration multiplier μ = 1/x − 2λ = 1/10 − 2/35 = 3/70 > 0, confirming the constraint binds
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Set ℒ = ln x + 2 ln y + λ(90 − 2x − 3y). The FOCs are 1/x − 2λ = 0, 2/y − 3λ = 0 and 2x + 3y = 90. From the first two, 2x = 1/λ and 3y = 2/λ, so spending on y is twice spending on x. With total spending 90, 2x = 30 and 3y = 60, giving x = 15, y = 20 and λ = 1/(2x) = 1/30.

(b) In general the same steps give pₓx = m/3 and pᵧy = 2m/3, so x = m/(3pₓ) and y = 2m/(3pᵧ). Maximised utility is V = ln(m/3pₓ) + 2 ln(2m/3pᵧ), so dV/dm = 1/m + 2/m = 3/m. At m = 90 this is 1/30 = λ, as the envelope theorem predicts: λ is the marginal utility of income.

(c) With Uₓₓ = −1/x², Uᵧᵧ = −2/y² and Uₓᵧ = 0, the bordered Hessian is [[0, 2, 3], [2, −1/x², 0], [3, 0, −2/y²]]. Expanding along the first row, its determinant is −2(−4/y²) + 3(3/x²) = 8/y² + 9/x² = 8/400 + 9/225 = 0.02 + 0.04 = 0.06 > 0. With two variables and one constraint, a positive sign confirms a local maximum. The objective is also concave, so the maximum is global.

(d) The unrationed choice x = 15 breaks the ration, so try x = 10 with the ration binding. The budget gives 3y = 90 − 20, so y = 70/3 ≈ 23.33. The Kuhn–Tucker FOCs with a multiplier μ on x ≤ 10 are 1/x − 2λ − μ = 0 and 2/y − 3λ = 0. From the second, λ = 2/(3y) = 2/70 = 1/35. Then μ = 1/10 − 2/35 = 7/70 − 4/70 = 3/70 > 0. Complementary slackness holds, and the positive μ is the shadow price of the ration: allowing one more unit of x would raise utility by about 3/70.

questions.q:
Leila has quasi-linear utility U = 2√x + y over a good x and money spent on everything else, y (price 1). The price of x is pₓ = 0.5, and her income m must satisfy 0.5x + y ≤ m, with x, y ≥ 0.

(a) Write the Kuhn–Tucker conditions for this problem. (4 marks)
(b) Solve for her demands and the multiplier when m = 6. (4 marks)
(c) Solve again when m = 1.5, showing which conditions now bind. (5 marks)
(d) Find the general demand for x as a function of pₓ and m, and explain what quasi-linearity implies for income effects and for consumer surplus as a welfare measure. (4 marks)
(e) Verify that λ is the marginal utility of income in each case. (3 marks)
markScheme: KT conditions: 1/√x − 0.5λ ≤ 0 with equality if x > 0; 1 − λ ≤ 0 with equality if y > 0
m = 6: interior y > 0 so λ = 1; then 1/√x = 0.5, x = 4; y = 6 − 2 = 4
m = 1.5: interior solution would need y = −0.5 < 0, so y = 0
Then x = 3 and λ = 2/√3 ≈ 1.155; the y-condition 1 − λ < 0 holds strictly
General demand: x = 1/pₓ² if m ≥ 1/pₓ; otherwise x = m/pₓ and y = 0
Interior demand does not depend on m: zero income effect on x
With zero income effects, CV = EV = ΔCS, so consumer surplus is exact
Envelope check: V = 2√(2m) at the corner gives dV/dm = 2/√(2m) = 2/√3 at m = 1.5; V = 2√4 + (m − 2) = m + 2 in the interior gives dV/dm = 1
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Let ℒ = 2√x + y + λ(m − 0.5x − y). The Kuhn–Tucker conditions are: ∂ℒ/∂x = 1/√x − 0.5λ ≤ 0, x ≥ 0, x·∂ℒ/∂x = 0; ∂ℒ/∂y = 1 − λ ≤ 0, y ≥ 0, y·∂ℒ/∂y = 0; and λ ≥ 0, 0.5x + y ≤ m, λ(m − 0.5x − y) = 0. Since the marginal utility of x is infinite at zero, x > 0, and the budget binds.

(b) With m = 6, try y > 0. Then 1 − λ = 0, so λ = 1, and 1/√x = 0.5 gives x = 4. The budget gives y = 6 − 2 = 4 > 0, confirming the guess.

(c) With m = 1.5, the same steps give x = 4 and y = 1.5 − 2 = −0.5, which is infeasible. So y = 0 and all income is spent on x: x = 1.5/0.5 = 3. The x-condition holds with equality, so λ = 2/√x = 2/√3 ≈ 1.155. The y-condition 1 − λ ≈ −0.155 < 0 holds strictly, which is consistent with y = 0.

(d) In general, an interior solution gives 1/√x = pₓ, so x = 1/pₓ², which requires m ≥ pₓx = 1/pₓ (here m ≥ 2). If income is below that, the corner applies: x = m/pₓ and y = 0. In the interior, demand for x does not depend on income: all extra income goes on y. With no income effect on x, Hicksian and Marshallian demands coincide, so CV = EV = ΔCS and consumer surplus is an exact money measure of welfare. At low incomes the corner restores an income effect.

(e) In the interior, V = 2√4 + (m − 2) = m + 2, so dV/dm = 1 = λ. At the corner, x = 2m and V = 2√(2m), so dV/dm = 2/√(2m), which equals 2/√3 at m = 1.5, again matching λ. λ is higher at the corner because extra income goes to x, which is worth more per pound than y.

questions.q:
Ashby Wind Ltd is valuing a small wind farm. Values are in £000s and the continuous discount rate is r.

(a) The farm earns a revenue stream R(t) = 2,000e^(0.02t) for 10 years. Find its present value when r = 0.06. (4 marks)
(b) A maintenance contract pays Ashby a rising stream S(t) = 100t for 5 years. Use integration by parts to find its present value when r = 0.1. (5 marks)
(c) In the regional market for green certificates, inverse demand is P = 113 − Q² and inverse supply is P = 5 + 2Q². Find the equilibrium and the consumer and producer surplus. (6 marks)
markScheme: Interprets: surplus shares reflect the relative curvature (supply steeper), producers get the larger share
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The discounted revenue is 2,000e^(0.02t)e^(−0.06t) = 2,000e^(−0.04t), so PV = ∫₀¹⁰ 2,000e^(−0.04t)dt = (2,000/0.04)(1 − e^(−0.4)) = 50,000 × (1 − 0.6703) ≈ 16,484, i.e. about £16.5m. The 2% growth effectively lowers the discount rate to 4%.

(b) PV = 100∫₀⁵ t·e^(−0.1t)dt. Let u = t and dv = e^(−0.1t)dt, so du = dt and v = −10e^(−0.1t). Then ∫t·e^(−0.1t)dt = −10t·e^(−0.1t) + 10∫e^(−0.1t)dt = −10t·e^(−0.1t) − 100e^(−0.1t) + C. Evaluating from 0 to 5: (−50e^(−0.5) − 100e^(−0.5)) − (0 − 100) = 100 − 150e^(−0.5) ≈ 100 − 90.98 = 9.02. Multiplying by 100, PV ≈ 902.0, i.e. about £902k. The undiscounted total is 100 × 5²/2 = 1,250, so discounting removes about 28% because most payments come late.

(c) Setting 113 − Q² = 5 + 2Q² gives 3Q² = 108, so Q* = 6 and P* = 113 − 36 = 77. Spending is 77 × 6 = 462. Consumer surplus is the area under demand minus spending: ∫₀⁶(113 − Q²)dQ = 678 − 72 = 606, so CS = 606 − 462 = 144. Producer surplus is spending minus the area under supply: ∫₀⁶(5 + 2Q²)dQ = 30 + 144 = 174, so PS = 462 − 174 = 288. Total surplus is 432. Producers capture two-thirds because supply rises twice as steeply in Q² as demand falls, so the gap between price and marginal cost is larger on the supply side. Linear triangle formulas would be wrong here because the curves are not straight lines.

questions.q:
The economy of Veloria is described by: Y = C + I + G, C = 100 + 0.8(Y − T) and T = 20 + 0.25Y, with investment I = 150 and government spending G = 200.

(a) Write the model as a matrix system Ax = b with x = (Y, C, T)ᵀ. (3 marks)
(b) Find det A and use Cramer's rule to find equilibrium income. (4 marks)
(c) Find equilibrium consumption and tax revenue, and check that the budget balance is G − T. (3 marks)
(d) Find the government spending multiplier dY/dG. (2 marks)
markScheme: Cramer for Y: replace column 1 by b, determinant = 434
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Rearranging each equation with the unknowns on the left: Y − C = I + G = 350; −0.8Y + C + 0.8T = 100; −0.25Y + T = 20. So A = [[1, −1, 0], [−0.8, 1, 0.8], [−0.25, 0, 1]] and b = (350, 100, 20)ᵀ.

(b) Expanding det A along the first row: 1 × (1 × 1 − 0.8 × 0) − (−1) × (−0.8 × 1 − 0.8 × (−0.25)) + 0 = 1 + (−0.8 + 0.2) = 0.4. In general det A = 1 − c + ct, where c = 0.8 is the marginal propensity to consume and t = 0.25 is the tax rate. Replacing the first column with b gives A₁ = [[350, −1, 0], [100, 1, 0.8], [20, 0, 1]]. Its determinant is 350(1) − (−1)(100 − 16) + 0 = 350 + 84 = 434. So Y* = 434/0.4 = 1,085.

(c) From the first equation, C* = Y* − 350 = 735. From the third, T* = 20 + 0.25 × 1,085 = 291.25. Check the consumption function: 100 + 0.8(1,085 − 291.25) = 100 + 0.8 × 793.75 = 735. The government budget balance G − T = 200 − 291.25 = −91.25, so the government runs a surplus of 91.25.

(d) G enters only the first element of b. By Cramer's rule, dY/dG is the (1, 1) cofactor of A divided by det A: (1 × 1 − 0.8 × 0)/0.4 = 2.5. Equivalently, dY/dG = 1/(1 − c(1 − t)) = 1/(1 − 0.6) = 2.5. The multiplier is smaller than the 1/(1 − 0.8) = 5 of a model without income tax, because taxes leak part of each round of spending.

questions.q:
A two-sector economy has agriculture (sector 1) and manufacturing (sector 2). Each £1 of agricultural output needs £0.20 of agricultural and £0.40 of manufactured inputs. Each £1 of manufacturing output needs £0.30 of agricultural and £0.10 of manufactured inputs. Final demand is £120m for agriculture and £60m for manufacturing.

(a) Write down the technical coefficient matrix A and the system for gross outputs. (3 marks)
(b) Find the Leontief inverse and the gross output of each sector. (5 marks)
(c) Check the Hawkins–Simon conditions and explain their meaning. (3 marks)
(d) Final demand for manufacturing rises by £30m. Find the change in each sector's output. Labour needs are 0.5 and 0.2 workers per £1,000 of output in sectors 1 and 2. Find total employment before the change. (4 marks)
markScheme: A = [[0.2, 0.3], [0.4, 0.1]] with column j giving inputs per £1 of sector j
Hawkins–Simon: diagonal elements of I − A positive and det(I − A) = 0.6 > 0, so the economy is productive and all outputs are non-negative
Interprets Leontief inverse entries as total (direct and indirect) requirements
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Column j of A lists inputs needed per £1 of sector j's output: A = [[0.2, 0.3], [0.4, 0.1]]. Gross output must cover inter-industry use plus final demand: x = Ax + d, so (I − A)x = d with I − A = [[0.8, −0.3], [−0.4, 0.9]] and d = (120, 60)ᵀ.

(b) det(I − A) = 0.8 × 0.9 − 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.72 − 0.12 = 0.6. The inverse is (1/0.6)[[0.9, 0.3], [0.4, 0.8]] = [[1.5, 0.5], [2/3, 4/3]]. Then x₁ = 1.5 × 120 + 0.5 × 60 = 210 and x₂ = (2/3) × 120 + (4/3) × 60 = 80 + 80 = 160, in £m. Check: agriculture supplies 0.2 × 210 + 0.3 × 160 = 90 to industry plus 120 to final demand, which is 210. Manufacturing supplies 0.4 × 210 + 0.1 × 160 = 100 plus 60, which is 160.

(c) The Hawkins–Simon conditions require the leading principal minors of I − A to be positive: 0.8 > 0 and det = 0.6 > 0. Both hold. Economically, each sector uses less than £1 of inputs per £1 of output, directly and indirectly, so the economy can meet any non-negative final demand with non-negative gross outputs. All entries of the Leontief inverse are positive.

(d) Δx = (I − A)⁻¹(0, 30)ᵀ = (0.5 × 30, (4/3) × 30) = (15, 40). Manufacturing output rises by more than £30m because manufacturing needs its own output as an input, and agriculture rises by £15m because it supplies manufacturing. The second column of the Leontief inverse gives these total requirements per £1 of final demand for manufactures. Before the change, output is £210m and £160m, so employment is 0.5 × 210,000 + 0.2 × 160,000 = 105,000 + 32,000 = 137,000 workers.

questions.q:
In the market for artisan bread in a market town, demand is Qd = 60 − 2P and supply is Qs = −15 + 3P. When the market is out of equilibrium, price adjusts according to dP/dt = 0.5(Qd − Qs). Initially P(0) = 23.

(a) Find the equilibrium price and quantity. (2 marks)
(b) Write the differential equation for P and solve it. (4 marks)
(c) Find the price after one period and the time taken for half of the initial gap to close. (3 marks)
(d) State the general condition for stability with linear demand Qd = α − βP and supply Qs = γ + δP, and explain it. (3 marks)
markScheme: Rewrites as dP/dt + 2.5P = 37.5 with steady state 15
General: dP/dt = k[(α − γ) − (β + δ)P], stable iff k(β + δ) > 0

With k > 0 this holds for normal slopes; instability needs supply to slope downward and respond more to price than demand (δ < −β); with price on the vertical axis that supply curve is flatter than demand
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Setting 60 − 2P = −15 + 3P gives 5P = 75, so P* = 15 and Q* = 30.

(b) Substituting, dP/dt = 0.5[(60 − 2P) − (−15 + 3P)] = 0.5(75 − 5P) = 37.5 − 2.5P. In standard form dP/dt + 2.5P = 37.5. The steady state is 37.5/2.5 = 15, and the homogeneous solution is Ae^(−2.5t). So P(t) = 15 + Ae^(−2.5t). Using P(0) = 23 gives A = 8, so P(t) = 15 + 8e^(−2.5t).

(c) After one period, P(1) = 15 + 8e^(−2.5) ≈ 15 + 8 × 0.0821 ≈ 15.66. The initial excess supply drives the price down quickly. The gap halves when e^(−2.5t) = 0.5, at t = ln 2/2.5 ≈ 0.28 periods. Each period the gap shrinks by a factor of e^(−2.5) ≈ 0.08, so after one period it is about 8% of its starting value.

(d) In general dP/dt = k[(α − βP) − (γ + δP)] = k(α − γ) − k(β + δ)P. The solution is P(t) = P* + (P(0) − P*)e^(−k(β + δ)t), with P* = (α − γ)/(β + δ). It converges if and only if k(β + δ) > 0. With k > 0 (price rises under excess demand), stability requires β + δ > 0: excess demand Qd − Qs must fall as price rises. This holds automatically for a downward-sloping demand curve and an upward-sloping supply curve. It can fail only if supply slopes downward and quantity supplied falls faster with price than quantity demanded does (δ < −β), so that a higher price widens excess demand. With price on the vertical axis, such a supply curve is flatter than the demand curve. The speed of adjustment depends on k and on how responsive the two sides of the market are.

questions.q:
In a Solow economy, capital per worker evolves according to k' = s·k^α − (n + δ)k, with saving rate s = 0.2, α = 0.5 and n + δ = 0.05. Initially k(0) = 4.

(a) Find the steady-state capital, output and consumption per worker. (4 marks)
(b) Use a phase-diagram argument and a derivative test to show the steady state is stable. (4 marks)
(c) Using the substitution z = k^(1−α), transform the equation into a linear differential equation in z and solve it for k(t). (6 marks)
(d) Find k after 20 years and the half-life of the gap in z. (3 marks)
(e) Find the golden-rule capital stock and saving rate, and comment on whether this economy saves too little or too much. (3 marks)
markScheme: Steady state: s·k^0.5 = 0.05k gives k^0.5 = 4, so k* = 16
k' > 0 below k* and k' < 0 above it because s·k^α is concave and cuts (n + δ)k from above
Derivative of k' at k*: 0.2 × 0.5 × 16^(−0.5) − 0.05 = −0.025 < 0, so stable
Linear first-order: steady state z* = 4, z(t) = 4 + (z(0) − 4)e^(−0.025t)
Golden rule: MPK = n + δ, 0.5k^(−0.5) = 0.05 gives k_G = 100 and s_G = α = 0.5
s = 0.2 < 0.5, so the economy saves too little; raising s would raise long-run consumption but with a short-run cost
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) In the steady state k' = 0, so 0.2k^0.5 = 0.05k, which gives k^0.5 = 4 and k* = 16. Output is y* = 16^0.5 = 4 and consumption is c* = 0.8 × 4 = 3.2.

(b) Saving s·k^0.5 is increasing and concave, starting at the origin with infinite slope, while break-even investment (n + δ)k is a straight line. They cross once at k* > 0. Below k*, saving exceeds break-even investment, so k' > 0; above k*, k' < 0. So k moves towards k* from either side. Formally, d(k')/dk = sαk^(α−1) − (n + δ) = 0.2 × 0.5 × 0.25 − 0.05 = −0.025 < 0 at k*, which confirms local stability.

(c) This is a Bernoulli equation. Let z = k^(1−α) = k^0.5. Then z' = 0.5k^(−0.5)k' = 0.5k^(−0.5)(0.2k^0.5 − 0.05k) = 0.1 − 0.025k^0.5 = 0.1 − 0.025z. This is linear: z' + 0.025z = 0.1, with steady state z* = 4 (matching √16) and solution z(t) = 4 + (z(0) − 4)e^(−0.025t). With k(0) = 4, z(0) = 2, so z(t) = 4 − 2e^(−0.025t) and k(t) = (4 − 2e^(−0.025t))².

(d) At t = 20, z = 4 − 2e^(−0.5) ≈ 4 − 1.213 = 2.787, so k ≈ 7.77, still well below 16. The gap in z halves every ln 2/0.025 ≈ 27.7 years. Convergence speed is (1 − α)(n + δ) = 2.5% a year, so the transition is slow.

(e) Across steady states, consumption is c = k^α − (n + δ)k, which is maximised where MPK = αk^(α−1) = n + δ. So 0.5k^(−0.5) = 0.05, giving k^0.5 = 10 and k_G = 100. The saving rate that delivers it is s_G = (n + δ)k_G/k_G^0.5 = 0.05 × 100/10 = 0.5 = α. Here s = 0.2 < 0.5, so the economy is dynamically efficient but saves too little to maximise steady-state consumption. Raising saving would lower consumption at first and raise it in the long run, so whether it is desirable depends on how the future is discounted.

questions.q:
A competitive firm has production function q = K^a L^b with a, b > 0, faces output price p and input prices r (capital) and w (labour).

(a) Derive the first-order conditions for profit maximisation and show that, at an interior optimum, rK = a·pq and wL = b·pq. (5 marks)
(b) Show that the Hessian of the profit function is negative definite if and only if a + b < 1. Explain what happens when a + b ≥ 1. (6 marks)
(c) Let a = 0.25, b = 0.5, p = 16, w = 2 and r = 1. Find the optimal inputs, output and profit. (5 marks)
(d) Use the envelope theorem to find dπ*/dp at these values and interpret the result. (4 marks)
markScheme: FOCs: a·pq/K = r and b·pq/L = w
Rearranging gives rK = a·pq and wL = b·pq: input shares equal the exponents
π_KK = a(a − 1)pq/K², π_LL = b(b − 1)pq/L², π_KL = ab·pq/(KL)
π_KK < 0 needs a < 1; |H| = (pq)²/(K²L²)·ab(1 − a − b), positive iff a + b < 1
a + b = 1: profit is homogeneous of degree 1 in inputs, so profit is zero or unbounded and there is no unique interior optimum; a + b > 1: no maximum (profit unbounded)
With the numbers, ratio of FOCs gives L = (b·r/(a·w))K = K
Interpretation: a £1 rise in price raises profit by about £64, with input re-optimisation having no first-order effect
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Profit is π = pK^a L^b − rK − wL. The FOCs are ∂π/∂K = a·pK^(a−1)L^b − r = 0 and ∂π/∂L = b·pK^a L^(b−1) − w = 0. Since K^(a−1)L^b = q/K, these become a·pq/K = r and b·pq/L = w, so rK = a·pq and wL = b·pq. Each input's share of revenue equals its exponent, and the profit share is 1 − a − b.

(b) The second derivatives are π_KK = a(a − 1)pq/K², π_LL = b(b − 1)pq/L² and π_KL = ab·pq/(KL). Then |H| = (pq)²/(K²L²)[ab(a − 1)(b − 1) − a²b²] = (pq)²/(K²L²)·ab(1 − a − b). Negative definiteness needs π_KK < 0 (so a < 1) and |H| > 0, which holds if and only if a + b < 1. With constant returns (a + b = 1), scaling both inputs scales profit, so profit is either zero everywhere along a ray or can be increased without limit: there is no unique optimum and firm size is indeterminate. With increasing returns there is no maximum at all. Decreasing returns are needed for a well-defined competitive firm.

(c) Dividing the FOCs gives (a/b)(L/K) = r/w, so L = (b·r/(a·w))K = (0.5 × 1/(0.25 × 2))K = K. The capital FOC becomes 0.25 × 16 × K^(−0.75) × K^0.5 = 4K^(−0.25) = 1, so K^0.25 = 4 and K = L = 256. Output is q = 256^0.75 = 64, revenue is 1,024 and cost is 256 + 512 = 768, giving profit 256. Shares check: rK/pq = 0.25, wL/pq = 0.5, profit share 0.25.

(d) By the envelope theorem (Hotelling's lemma), dπ*/dp = ∂π/∂p evaluated at the optimum, which is q* = 64. If the output price rises by £1, profit rises by about £64. The firm will also change its inputs, but because it was already optimising, those changes have no first-order effect on profit. Over larger price changes profit rises faster than this linear estimate, because the profit function is convex in p.

questions.q:
In the market for e-bikes in a UK region, demand is Q = A·P^(−1.2)·Y^0.8 and supply is Q = B·P^0.4, where Y is average household income and A, B > 0 are constants.

(a) Taking logs, write the equilibrium as a linear system in ln P and ln Q. (3 marks)
(b) Use implicit differentiation or Cramer's rule to find the income elasticities of equilibrium price and quantity. (5 marks)
(c) Income rises by 10%. Estimate the percentage changes in price and quantity using the elasticities, and give the exact changes. (4 marks)
(d) For general differentiable demand D(P, Y) and supply S(P), derive dP*/dY using the implicit function theorem and state the conditions for it to be positive. (3 marks)
markScheme: ln Q = ln A − 1.2 ln P + 0.8 ln Y and ln Q = ln B + 0.4 ln P
System: ln Q + 1.2 ln P = ln A + 0.8 ln Y; ln Q − 0.4 ln P = ln B
Eliminating ln Q: 1.6 ln P = ln A − ln B + 0.8 ln Y
F(P, Y) = D(P, Y) − S(P) = 0 gives dP*/dY = −F_Y/F_P = D_Y/(S_P − D_P)
Positive if the good is normal (D_Y > 0) and S_P − D_P > 0 (upward supply, downward demand)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Taking logs of both equations: ln Q = ln A − 1.2 ln P + 0.8 ln Y and ln Q = ln B + 0.4 ln P. In matrix form, [[1, 1.2], [1, −0.4]](ln Q, ln P)ᵀ = (ln A + 0.8 ln Y, ln B)ᵀ. The constant-elasticity forms become linear in logs.

(b) The determinant of the coefficient matrix is −0.4 − 1.2 = −1.6. By Cramer's rule, ln P = [1 × ln B − 1 × (ln A + 0.8 ln Y)]/(−1.6) = (ln A − ln B + 0.8 ln Y)/1.6. So the income elasticity of price is d ln P/d ln Y = 0.8/1.6 = 0.5. Substituting into supply, ln Q = ln B + 0.4 ln P, so d ln Q/d ln Y = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2. In general, the price elasticity is η/(ε + θ), where η is the income elasticity of demand, ε = 1.2 the absolute price elasticity of demand and θ = 0.4 the supply elasticity.

(c) Using the elasticities, a 10% income rise raises price by about 5% and quantity by about 2%. Because the model is exactly linear in logs, the exact changes are P₁/P₀ = 1.1^0.5 ≈ 1.0488, a rise of 4.88%, and Q₁/Q₀ = 1.1^0.2 ≈ 1.0192, a rise of 1.92%. The approximations are close because 10% is a modest change. Price takes most of the adjustment because supply is inelastic relative to demand.

(d) Define F(P, Y) = D(P, Y) − S(P) = 0 in equilibrium. By the implicit function theorem, dP*/dY = −F_Y/F_P = −D_Y/(D_P − S_P) = D_Y/(S_P − D_P), provided F_P ≠ 0. With D_P < 0 and S_P > 0 the denominator is positive, so price rises with income if and only if the good is normal (D_Y > 0). The effect is larger the less price-responsive both demand and supply are.
